meta.blurb: A shepherd, a stormy night, a deer by a stream, exiles weeping by a river. The Book of Psalms holds 150 ancient songs of joy, fear, doubt and hope. Read its best-loved poems, one at a time, from the first to the last.
meta.bible: Book of Psalms: a book of the Hebrew Bible, also part of the Christian Old Testament, with 150 poems, songs and prayers from ancient Israel. Psalm and Psalms. Hebrew: the language of the original. Tehillim: the Hebrew name, meaning praises. Israel: the ancient kingdom and people. Jerusalem. Zion: the hill of Jerusalem, a name for the city. Judah: the land around Jerusalem, with its dry desert. Babylon: the city that took many people of Judah away as captives. Egypt. David: the king of Israel to whom tradition links many psalms, once a shepherd. Absalom: David's son, who rose up against him. Saul: the king before David. Bathsheba. Nathan: the prophet who spoke to David. Solomon: David's son and a later king. Moses: the leader linked with Psalm 90. Aaron: Moses's brother and the first priest. Asaph: a singer linked with Psalm 73 and others. Korah: the sons of Korah are named in the titles of several psalms. Hermon: a high mountain. The Lord: the name that most English translations use for the name of God. God. Most High. Torah: the first five books of the Bible. Jews. Jewish. Christians. Christian. Gospels. Jesus. Bible. Acrostic: a poem whose lines begin with the letters of the alphabet in order. Ashrei: a Jewish prayer that includes Psalm 145. Songs of Ascents: Psalms 120 to 134, sung by pilgrims. Psalm 1: the happy person like a tree. Psalm 23: the shepherd. Psalm 51: the prayer for a clean heart. Psalm 90: the prayer of Moses. Psalm 117: the shortest chapter. Psalm 119: the longest chapter, 176 verses. Psalm 136: the refrain. Psalm 137: by the rivers of Babylon. Psalm 150: the last psalm. Voice and tone: calm, warm, clear and respectful. Every idea is attributed to the psalm it comes from. The words are retold, never long quotations. Where a psalm can be read in more than one way, or is difficult, say so. Never preach or compare faiths.

B1B2: The Book of Psalms is a collection of 150 songs and prayers from ancient Israel. In Hebrew it is called Tehillim, which means praises, although many of the psalms are about sorrow too.
The psalms are arranged in five sections, like the five books of Moses. Each section ends with a short blessing, and the last psalm serves as a grand closing song for the whole collection.
Many psalms have a title that names a person, such as David, Asaph or the sons of Korah. Tradition says that King David wrote many of them, but scholars think the collection grew over many centuries.
Hebrew poetry does not rhyme the way many English songs do. Instead, a second line often repeats or answers the first, so that the same idea is seen from two sides.

Psalm 1 opens the book with a picture of a happy person who loves the teaching of God. That person is like a tree beside flowing water, which gives its fruit on time, while the wicked are like dry chaff blown away.

The title of Psalm 3 says that David wrote it while he was running away from his son Absalom. Even with many enemies around him, the singer lies down, sleeps and wakes again, because he trusts that God is protecting him.
Psalm 8 looks up at the moon and the stars and asks what a human being is, that God should care. Then it answers that people have been given a place of honour and care over the animals of the earth.

Psalm 13 begins with the cry how long, asked four times, as the singer wonders when God will stop seeming to forget him. By the end, however, he says that he trusts God's love and will sing because God has been good to him.

Psalm 15 asks who may stay in God's tent and live on his holy hill. The answer is a list of everyday habits: telling the truth, not spreading rumours, keeping promises, and not taking advantage of the poor.

Psalm 18, whose title connects it with David's escape from Saul, calls God a rock, a fortress and a shield. It pictures God answering in a great storm of thunder and fire, and leading the singer out to a wide, open place.

Psalm 19 says that the heavens declare the glory of God, and that day after day the sky pours out its message without a word. The second half praises God's teaching as more precious than gold and sweeter than honey.

Psalm 22 opens with a terrible cry, asking why God has left the singer alone. The poem goes on to describe pain and mocking crowds, but it ends with the hope that all nations will remember and praise God.
Psalm 23, perhaps the best known of all, says that the Lord is my shepherd, and that the singer will lack nothing. The shepherd leads him to green grass and quiet water, and gives him new strength.

Even when the path leads through a very dark valley, the singer says that he is not afraid, because the shepherd is with him. Then the picture changes to a feast, where his enemies watch as God fills his cup.
Psalm 24 begins by saying that the whole earth belongs to God. Then the singers call on the ancient gates to lift up their heads and open, so that the king of glory may come in.
Psalm 34 invites everyone to taste and see that God is good. It is also an acrostic poem, in which the verses begin with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order.
Psalm 27 begins by asking whom the singer should fear, since God is his light and his strength. Even if an army camps against him, he says, his heart will not be afraid.
Psalm 30 is a song of thanks from someone who has been rescued from trouble and sorrow. It says that weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes with the morning.
Psalm 32 describes how heavy it felt to hide a wrong, as the singer's strength dried up while he kept silent. When he finally told God what he had done, he says, he was forgiven and felt happy again.
Psalm 37 advises the reader not to be upset by people who do wrong and seem to succeed. They will fade quickly like grass, it says, while those who trust God and are gentle will inherit the land.
Psalm 40 says that the singer waited patiently for God, who lifted him out of a muddy pit and set his feet on a rock. God then gave him a new song, and he hopes that many will hear it and trust.
Psalm 42 compares the singer's longing for God to a deer that pants for streams of water. He is sad and far from home, and he asks his own soul why it is so downcast, and tells it to hope.
Psalm 46 says that God is a refuge and a strength, a help that is always ready in trouble. Even if the earth shakes and the mountains fall into the sea, the singers say, they will not be afraid.
The title of Psalm 51 links it to David and the prophet Nathan, who told the king that he had done wrong. In it the singer asks God for mercy, asks to be washed clean, and asks for a pure heart.

Psalm 63, whose title places it in the dry desert of Judah, says that the singer's soul thirsts for God like dry land without water. At night, he says, he remembers God, and he sings in the shadow of God's wings.
Psalm 65 is a harvest song that thanks God for the rain that waters the earth. The fields are full of grain, the hills are covered with flocks, and the whole land seems to shout and sing for joy.
Psalm 72, whose title names Solomon, is a prayer for a king to rule with justice. It asks that he defend the poor, rescue the needy, and be like rain falling on a field that has just been cut.

In Psalm 73, a singer named Asaph almost loses his faith because the wicked seem to live easy, happy lives. Everything changes when he enters the sanctuary of God, and he realises that nothing on earth matters to him more than God.

Psalm 78 is a long poem that retells the history of Israel, from the escape from Egypt to the choosing of David. Its purpose, it says, is to tell the next generation what God has done, so that they will not forget.
Psalm 84 says how lovely God's dwelling place is, and how much the singer longs to be there. Even the sparrow and the swallow have found a home near it, where they can raise their young.
Psalm 88 is often called the darkest of all the psalms, because it never turns to hope. It ends with the singer saying that darkness is his closest friend, and many readers value its honesty.
Psalm 90 is the only psalm whose title names Moses. It says that a thousand years are like yesterday to God, and it asks God to teach us to count our days so that we may gain wisdom.

Psalm 91 describes the person who lives in the shelter of the Most High as safe under his wings. It speaks of fear by night, arrows by day, and danger on every side, and it promises that God will be a refuge.
Psalm 100 is a short song of thanks for all the earth to sing. It calls people to serve God with gladness, to enter his gates with thanks, and to remember that his love lasts for ever.
Psalm 103 tells the singer's own soul to bless God and not to forget his kindness. As far as the east is from the west, it says, so far does God remove our wrongs from us.

Psalm 104 is a long poem about creation, in which God waters the hills, feeds the animals, and provides the wine, oil and bread that people enjoy. It names wild goats on the mountains, birds in the trees and ships on the sea.

Psalm 117 is the shortest chapter in the Bible, with only two verses that call all nations to praise God. Psalm 119 is the longest, with 176 verses, and it praises God's teaching from beginning to end.
Psalm 121 begins by looking up at the hills and asking where help will come from. The answer is that it comes from God, who made heaven and earth, and who never sleeps while he watches over you.

Psalms 120 to 134 are called the Songs of Ascents, and pilgrims probably sang them as they climbed to Jerusalem for the festivals. In Psalm 122, the singer says he was glad when the others said, let us go to the house of God.

Psalm 126 remembers the day when the captives came home, and it says that people were like dreamers, laughing and singing. It ends with the promise that those who sow with tears will reap with songs of joy.
Psalm 127 says that unless the Lord builds the house, the builders work in vain. In the same way, getting up early and staying up late is pointless without God, who gives sleep to those he loves.
In Psalm 131, the singer says that his heart is not proud and that he does not chase after great things. Like a small child resting in its mother's arms, his soul is quiet and calm.

Psalm 133 is only three verses long, yet it says how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity. It compares this peace to fine oil running down the beard of Aaron, and to the dew on Mount Hermon.

In Psalm 136, each of the 26 verses ends with the same refrain, his love endures for ever. Scholars think that a leader sang the first half of each line, and that the people answered with the refrain.

Psalm 137 was written by people taken as prisoners to Babylon, who sat by its rivers and wept when they remembered Zion. It ends with angry calls for revenge, which readers find hard, and which show how deep their pain was.

Psalm 139 says that God has searched the singer and knows him completely, from his sitting down to his rising up. There is nowhere he could go, not even the far side of the sea, where God would not be.
Psalm 145 is another alphabet poem, and it praises God as kind, merciful and slow to become angry. It says that the eyes of all creatures look to him, and that he opens his hand and feeds them.

Psalm 148 calls on everything to praise God, from the sun, moon and stars to the great creatures of the deep. Fire, hail, mountains, trees, wild animals, kings and children are all invited to join in.

The last psalm is a burst of joyful noise, calling on people to praise God with trumpet, harp, drum, strings, pipe and loud cymbals. It ends by saying that everything that has breath should praise God.

For more than two thousand years, Jews and Christians have sung, chanted and prayed the psalms in worship, at home, and in times of grief and joy. Their honest mix of praise, sorrow, doubt and hope still speaks to many people today.
C1C2: The Book of Psalms, which belongs to the Hebrew Bible, is a collection of 150 poems, songs and prayers that were gathered over many centuries in ancient Israel. Its Hebrew name, Tehillim, means praises, although a good many of the psalms are cries of grief, doubt and anger rather than songs of joy. Jews and Christians have both treasured the collection, and it remains one of the most widely read and sung books of the whole Bible.

The psalms are arranged in five sections, which many scholars believe were meant to echo the five books of the Law of Moses. Each of the first four sections closes with a short blessing of God, and the whole of the last psalm serves as a grand closing song for the entire collection. This structure suggests that the book was shaped with care, rather than gathered at random.

About seventy of the psalms carry the name of David in their titles, and tradition remembers him as Israel's shepherd boy, singer and king. Others are linked with Asaph, with the sons of Korah, with Solomon and even with Moses, who is named in the title of Psalm 90. Most scholars think that the collection grew over many centuries, and that the titles may record how the psalms were remembered and used rather than who actually wrote them.

Hebrew poetry does not depend on rhyme but on a kind of balance, in which a second line repeats, extends or answers the first so that an idea is viewed from two sides. Alongside this, the psalms fall into recognisable kinds, such as songs of praise, laments, prayers of thanks, poems about wisdom, and songs about kings. Knowing which kind of psalm one is reading, many readers find, makes it much easier to understand what it is doing.

Psalm 1 stands at the door of the whole book, and it describes a happy person who does not follow the counsel of the wicked but delights in the teaching of God and thinks about it day and night. Such a person is like a tree planted beside streams of water, which yields its fruit in season and whose leaf does not wither. The wicked, by contrast, are like chaff, the light husk of grain, which the wind carries away without a trace.

In Psalm 3, whose title connects it with David's flight from his son Absalom, the singer speaks of a great crowd rising up against him and of those who say that God will not help him. Yet he calls God a shield around him, and he says that he lay down and slept, and woke again, because the Lord sustained him. The next psalm, which readers have long treated as an evening prayer, says in a similar spirit that it is God alone who lets the singer lie down in peace and sleep.

Looking up at the moon and the stars that God has set in place, the singer of Psalm 8 wonders aloud what a human being is, that anyone so great should notice such a small creature. Yet the psalm answers its own wonder by declaring that people have been crowned with glory and honour, and given care of the sheep, the wild animals, the birds and the fish. It is a poem of astonishment, which holds the smallness and the dignity of human life in a single breath.

The short Psalm 13 opens with the cry how long, repeated four times, as the singer asks how long God will seem to have forgotten him, how long he must carry sorrow in his heart, and how long his enemy will win. It is an honest lament, in which no feeling is hidden or made to sound more polite than it is. Yet in its last lines the mood turns, and the singer declares that he trusts in God's steady love and will sing because God has been good to him.

Psalm 15 asks who may stay in the tent of God and live on his holy hill, and the answer that it gives is surprisingly practical. The person it describes speaks the truth from the heart, does not spread rumours about a neighbour, keeps a promise even when it costs something, and refuses to take advantage of the poor. Closeness to God, in this psalm, is shown as much in honest everyday conduct as in worship.

Psalm 18, whose title connects it with the day that David was rescued from his enemies and from King Saul, piles up names for God: my rock, my fortress, my shield and my deliverer. It then imagines God answering the cry for help in a terrifying storm, with the earth shaking, smoke rising, thunder crashing and hailstones falling. In the end the singer is carried out of danger into a wide and open place, and he says that God rescued him because God delighted in him.

The first half of Psalm 19 is a hymn to the sky, in which the heavens declare the glory of God and one day passes the message on to the next, even though there is no speech and no sound. The sun comes out like a bridegroom from his tent, it says, and nothing is hidden from its warmth. The second half turns to God's teaching, which is described as perfect, trustworthy, more precious than gold and sweeter than honey from the comb.

Psalm 22 begins with one of the most piercing cries in the Bible, asking why God has abandoned the singer and is so far from his groaning. The poem describes weakness, mocking crowds and fear without softening any of it, and then its tone changes as the singer declares that God has not despised the suffering of the afflicted. Christian tradition remembers that the Gospels put its opening words on the lips of Jesus, while the psalm itself ends with the hope that every nation will remember and turn to God.

Psalm 23, probably the best known of all the psalms, begins with the calm statement that the Lord is my shepherd, and that the singer therefore lacks nothing. The shepherd makes his sheep lie down in fresh green pastures and leads them beside quiet waters, restoring their strength when they are tired. In a land of dry hills, where grass and water make the difference between life and death, the picture of such care is deeply moving.

The path of the shepherd does not avoid hard places, for the psalm speaks of walking through the valley of deep darkness, or, as older translations have it, the valley of the shadow of death, where the singer will fear no evil because the shepherd is with him. Then the picture changes, and God becomes a host who sets a table in the presence of enemies, anoints the guest's head with oil and fills his cup until it overflows. The psalm closes with the confidence that goodness and mercy will follow the singer all the days of his life, and that he will live in the house of God for ever.

Psalm 24 opens with the grand claim that the earth and everything in it belong to God, who founded it upon the seas. It then asks who may climb the hill of the Lord, and answers that it is the person with clean hands and a pure heart. Many scholars think that the final verses were sung as a procession arrived at the gates of Jerusalem, with one voice calling on the ancient doors to lift up their heads and another asking who the king of glory might be.

Psalm 34 invites its readers to taste and see that the Lord is good, as though God's goodness were something that could be tested at the table. It says that God is close to the brokenhearted and rescues those whose spirits are crushed, and it adds that the righteous may have many troubles but are delivered from them all. The psalm is also an acrostic, with its verses beginning with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet, which made it easier to memorise and gave it a feeling of completeness.

Psalm 27 begins with a pair of rhetorical questions: the Lord is my light and my salvation, so whom shall I fear, and the Lord is the stronghold of my life, so of whom shall I be afraid? Even if an army were to camp against him, the singer says, his heart would not be afraid, and he asks for one thing above all, to live in the house of God and to look on its beauty. The psalm closes with advice that is addressed to the reader as much as to the singer, which is to wait for the Lord, to be strong and to take heart.

Psalm 30 is a song of thanksgiving from someone who has been brought back from the edge of the grave, and whose title connects it with the dedication of the temple. It declares that God's anger lasts only a moment while his favour lasts a lifetime, and that weeping may linger for the night but joy comes with the morning. The singer remembers feeling so safe that he thought he could never be shaken, and then recalls how quickly that confidence vanished, until God turned his mourning into dancing.

Psalm 32 opens by calling happy the person whose wrongdoing has been forgiven, and then it describes how that happiness was found. While the singer kept silent about his guilt, he says, his bones wasted away and his strength dried up as in the heat of summer, but when he finally confessed, God forgave him. The psalm closes with a gentle invitation to trust, advising people not to be stubborn like a horse or a mule, but to learn from God's counsel and to rejoice.

Psalm 37 begins with some practical advice: do not fret because of those who do wrong, and do not envy people who seem to succeed by evil means, for they will soon fade like grass and wither like green plants. Those who trust in the Lord, who are gentle and who wait patiently, it says, will inherit the land and find delight in great peace. In a memorable line the singer, now old, says that in a long life he has never seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread.

Psalm 40 begins by recalling a long and patient wait, at the end of which God turned to the singer, lifted him out of a pit of mud and mire, and set his feet on solid rock. In place of his old complaints he was given a new song, a song of praise, and he says that many who see it will be moved to trust in God. The psalm then adds that God does not want sacrifices as much as an open ear and a willing heart, and that the singer takes delight in doing his will.

Psalm 42 opens with one of the most famous images in the book, a deer panting for streams of water, which stands for the singer's thirst for God. He is far from the place of worship, he remembers happier days among the crowds who walked with him to the house of God, and his tears have become his food day and night. Three times he speaks to his own soul, asking why it is so downcast and telling it to put its hope in God, which shows how a person can argue gently with despair.

Psalm 46 declares that God is a refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble, and it imagines the worst that might happen: the earth giving way, the mountains toppling into the sea and the waters roaring. Yet beside the city of God there flows a quiet river that brings gladness, and the city, because God is within it, will not fall. In the midst of the noise of nations comes a calm command, be still and know that I am God, which has comforted readers in many ages.

The title of Psalm 51 connects it with David, at the time when the prophet Nathan came to him after he had done a serious wrong, and the psalm has become the classic prayer of repentance. The singer asks for mercy, admits his fault without excuse, and begs to be washed clean, and in its best-known line he asks God to create in him a clean heart and to renew a steady spirit within him. The sacrifice that God truly wants, he says, is a broken and humble spirit, which God will not despise.

Psalm 63, whose title places it in the wilderness of Judah, begins with an earnest cry: God, you are my God, and my soul thirsts for you in a dry and weary land where there is no water. The singer remembers seeing God's power in the sanctuary, and he says that God's steady love is better than life itself. Even in the long hours of the night, he lies awake thinking of God, and he sings in the shadow of God's wings.

Psalm 65 is a song of thanksgiving for the harvest, in which God is pictured as a gardener who visits the earth, waters its furrows and softens the ground with showers. The year is crowned with his bounty, the pastures are clothed with flocks and the valleys are wrapped in grain, until the whole land seems to shout and sing for joy. It is a reminder that ancient Israel lived close to the soil, and that the gift of rain and a good crop was never taken for granted.

Psalm 72, whose title connects it with Solomon, is a prayer for the king, asking that God give him justice so that he may judge the people fairly and defend the afflicted. Its picture of the ideal ruler is a gentle one, for he is like rain falling on a mown field, like showers that water the earth, and he rescues the needy who cry for help and has pity on the weak. The psalm closes the second of the five sections of the book, and its last verse notes that the prayers of David, son of Jesse, are ended.

In Psalm 73 the singer Asaph admits that his feet had almost slipped, because he envied the arrogant and watched the wicked grow rich and healthy while he himself struggled. The turning point comes when he enters the sanctuary of God and begins to see their lives from a longer point of view, which shows him how slippery their ground is. By the end he says that, with God, he has no wish for anything else in heaven or on earth, for even when his body and heart fail, God is the strength of his heart.

Psalm 78 is a long historical poem that begins with an invitation to listen to a teaching, a series of old riddles that the fathers handed down to their children so that each generation might tell the next. It then retells the story of the escape from Egypt, the years in the wilderness, the repeated failures of the people to trust, and the choice of David to be the shepherd of Israel. The point of the history is not to boast but to warn and encourage, so that later generations might set their hope in God and not forget his deeds.

Psalm 84 is the song of a pilgrim who longs for the courts of God, crying out that his heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God. Even the sparrow has found a home there, the singer says, and the swallow a nest for her young, near the very altar, and happy are all who live in that house. Those who pass through the dry valley of Baca, whose name may mean weeping or balsam trees, turn it into a place of springs, and the psalm ends with the claim that a single day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere.

Psalm 88 is often called the darkest of all the psalms, for it is a lament that never turns toward comfort, and its last words are that darkness has become the singer's closest companion. He describes himself as someone close to death, shut in and forgotten, who has cried out to God every day and has yet to hear a reply. Even so, he keeps speaking to God, and for that reason many readers value the psalm for its honesty and for showing that a faithful person may sometimes sit in silence and sorrow.

Psalm 90, the only psalm that is attributed in its title to Moses, begins by calling God a dwelling place for all generations and says that a thousand years in his sight are like yesterday when it is gone. By contrast, human life is as brief as grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening, and the usual span of a life, it says, is seventy years or perhaps eighty. In the face of such brevity, the prayer is not for despair but for wisdom: teach us to count our days so that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

Psalm 91 describes the one who lives in the shelter of the Most High as someone who rests in the shadow of the Almighty, covered by God's feathers and protected under his wings. It speaks of fear by night, arrows by day and sickness that stalks in the dark, and it promises that a thousand may fall beside the believer without harm coming near. Readers have taken these great promises in different ways, some as a literal guarantee and many as a poetic assurance that God is present in danger.

Psalm 100, whose title calls it a psalm of thanksgiving, is a short and joyful summons to all the earth to shout for joy, to serve the Lord with gladness and to come into his presence with singing. It reminds the singers that it is God who made us, and that we are his people, the sheep of his pasture. The call is to enter his gates with thanksgiving and his courts with praise, for his love endures for ever and his faithfulness to every generation.

Psalm 103 begins with a command to the singer's own soul to bless the Lord and not to forget any of his benefits, among them forgiveness, healing and a life crowned with love and compassion. As far as the east is from the west, it says, so far has God removed our wrongs from us, and as a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who respect him. Human life is brief, like grass or a wildflower, which the wind blows over and which is gone, yet the love of God, the psalm insists, lasts from age to age.

Psalm 104 is a sweeping hymn to creation, in which God stretches out the heavens like a tent, sends springs into the valleys and waters the hills so that the earth is satisfied with the fruit of his work. It looks closely at the wild goats of the high mountains, the birds nesting in the trees, the lions seeking their food, and the ships crossing the sea where the great creatures play. Every creature, the singer says, looks to God to give it food in due season, and when he hides his face they are terrified, but when he sends his breath, they are created and the earth is renewed.

Psalm 117 is the shortest chapter in the whole Bible, with only two verses, in which all nations and all peoples are called to praise the Lord for his great love toward us. Psalm 119, which comes soon afterwards, is by far the longest, with 176 verses arranged in twenty-two sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every verse in a section begins with the same letter. Its subject is the beauty of God's law, which the writer calls a lamp for his feet and a light for his path, and which he says he loves more than he can tell.

Psalm 121 begins as a traveller lifts his eyes to the hills and asks where his help will come from, and the answer is that it comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. The one who keeps you will not slumber, the psalm says, for the keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps, and he is a shade at your right hand, so that the sun will not harm you by day nor the moon by night. The poem ends by promising that God will guard your going out and your coming in, now and for ever.

Psalms 120 to 134 are called the Songs of Ascents, and many scholars believe that pilgrims sang them as they climbed the hills of Judah to Jerusalem for the great festivals. In Psalm 122 the singer says that he rejoiced when people said let us go to the house of the Lord, and he pictures at last the feet of the travellers standing inside the gates of the city. The psalm closes with a prayer for the peace of Jerusalem, which asks for security within its walls and prosperity within its towers, for the sake of family and friends.

Psalm 126 recalls the day when the Lord restored the fortunes of Zion and the returning captives were so happy that they felt as though they were dreaming, with laughter on their lips and songs on their tongues. Even the nations around them said that God had done great things for them, and the people agreed. The psalm then prays for a fresh restoration, like the streams that fill the dry riverbeds of the desert, and promises that those who sow in tears will reap with songs of joy and come home carrying their sheaves.

Psalm 127, whose title names Solomon, makes a quiet point about the limits of human effort: unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain, and unless he watches over the city, the guards stay awake for nothing. It is useless, the psalm says, to rise early and go late to bed, working anxiously for bread, since God gives sleep to those he loves. The second half turns to the family, calling children a gift from the Lord and a reward, like arrows in the hands of a warrior.

Psalm 131 is one of the shortest in the book, and one of the quietest, in which the singer says that his heart is not proud, his eyes are not haughty and he does not occupy himself with matters too great or too wonderful for him. Instead, he has calmed and quieted his soul, like a weaned child with its mother, resting in her arms without crying for anything. The psalm ends by turning to the whole people and telling them to put their hope in the Lord, both now and for ever.

Psalm 133 is only three verses long, yet it opens with a sentence that people still quote at weddings and in community gatherings, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity. Its first image is of precious oil poured on the head, running down the beard of Aaron and over the collar of his robes, and its second is of the dew of Mount Hermon falling on the hills of Zion. Both pictures speak of abundance that flows downward from above, and both suggest that unity is not forced but received as a blessing.

In Psalm 136, every one of the 26 verses ends with the same refrain, his love endures for ever, and scholars think that it was sung in turn, with a leader calling out each deed of God and the congregation answering with the response. The deeds that it recounts range from the making of the heavens, the earth, the sun, the moon and the stars to the rescue from Egypt, the crossing of the sea and the gift of a land. The constant return of the refrain makes the poem feel like waves coming in to shore, each one bringing the same message.

By the rivers of Babylon, begins Psalm 137, we sat down and wept when we remembered Zion, and the captives hung their harps on the poplar trees because their captors demanded songs of joy. How could they sing the songs of the Lord in a foreign land, they ask, and they vow that they will never forget Jerusalem, even if their right hand loses its skill. The final lines call for violent revenge on Babylon, which many readers find disturbing, but which shows how raw the pain of exile was, and the psalm does not hide it.

Psalm 139 begins with the thought that God has searched the singer and knows him through and through, understanding his thoughts from afar and knowing every word before it reaches his tongue. The singer then asks where he could go to escape this presence, and answers that if he climbed to heaven, or made his bed in the depths, or flew to the far side of the sea, God would be there too. It is also a psalm about the wonder of being a person, for it says that he was fearfully and wonderfully made, and knit together in his mother's womb.

Psalm 145 is another alphabetical poem, whose lines begin with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, and it praises God as gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in love. The Lord is good to all, it says, and his compassion is over all that he has made, so that the eyes of every creature look to him for food and he opens his hand to satisfy the desire of every living thing. In Jewish tradition this psalm forms the heart of a prayer called Ashrei, which is said three times a day.

Psalm 148 summons the whole of creation to praise, beginning in the heavens with the angels, the sun, the moon and the shining stars, and descending to the earth, where the great sea creatures, the fire and hail, the mountains, the fruit trees and the wild animals are all called to join. Kings, rulers and ordinary young men and women, old people and children are then invited to add their voices to the same song. The poem sees the world as a single choir, in which every part, from a star to a child, has something to offer.

The last psalm of the book is a burst of joyful noise, in which the reader is told to praise God in his sanctuary and in the heavens, for his mighty deeds and for his surpassing greatness. One instrument after another is called to join in, the trumpet, the harp and lyre, the tambourine and dancing, the strings and flute, and the clash of loud cymbals. The collection that began with a quiet person under a tree ends with a great chorus, and its final line says that everything that has breath should praise the Lord.

For more than two thousand years, Jews and Christians have sung, chanted and prayed the psalms in worship and at home, at weddings and funerals, in times of joy and in times of fear. What makes the collection endure is its honesty, for it makes room for thanks and for complaint, for confidence and for doubt, and it does not ask the singer to hide any feeling from God. Whatever one's own beliefs, the psalms remain a remarkable record of how human beings have put their deepest hopes and griefs into words.
